exercise_changes.old_statement:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{pb:jensen}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that for real $x$ and $\theta$ and $n\ge1$,
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(x^2-2x\cos\Bigl(\theta+\frac{2\pi k}n\Bigr)+1\Bigr)=x^{2n}-2x^n\cos n\theta+1.
\]
\item Deduce Poisson's integral: for $|x|\ne1$, $\int_0^\pi\log(1-2x\cos\theta+x^2)\dd\theta$ is $0$ if $|x|<1$ and
$2\pi\log|x|$ if $|x|>1$.
\item Let $P=a\prod_{k=1}^d(X-z_k)\in\C[X]$, $a\ne0$, with no root of modulus $1$. Show that
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log\bigl|P(e^{i\theta})\bigr|\dd\theta=\log|a|+\sum_{k=1}^d\log\max(1,|z_k|).
\]
What does Problem~\ref{pb:kronecker} say about the polynomials of $\Z[X]$ for which this is $0$?
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:jensen}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Show that for real $x$ and $\theta$ and $n\ge1$,
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(x^2-2x\cos\Bigl(\theta+\frac{2\pi k}n\Bigr)+1\Bigr)=x^{2n}-2x^n\cos n\theta+1.
\]
\item Deduce Poisson's integral: for $|x|\ne1$, $\int_0^\pi\log(1-2x\cos\theta+x^2)\dd\theta$ is $0$ if $|x|<1$ and
$2\pi\log|x|$ if $|x|>1$.
\item Let $P=a\prod_{k=1}^d(X-z_k)\in\C[X]$, $a\ne0$, with no root of modulus $1$. Show that
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log\bigl|P(e^{i\theta})\bigr|\dd\theta=\log|a|+\sum_{k=1}^d\log\max(1,|z_k|).
\]
What does Problem~\ref{pb:kronecker} say about the polynomials of $\Z[X]$ for which this is $0$?
\item Extend the formula to roots on the unit circle, interpreting the integral as an improper limit at the finitely many zero angles. Characterize the integer polynomials with zero mean in this extended case.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

exercise_changes.old_statement:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:dodecaturns}
\emph{Random turns of an icosahedron.} The rotation group of the regular icosahedron is isomorphic to $A_5$ (Theorem~12.5), and the
$20$ rotations by a third of a turn about the axes through the centres of opposite faces form the conjugacy class of the
$3$-cycles. An icosahedron is turned, again and again, by a uniformly chosen one of these $20$ rotations.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $\mu$ be a probability on a finite group $G$ that is constant on conjugacy classes, and $\mu^{*t}$ the law of the walk at time
$t$, started at $e$. Show that, for every $g\in G$,
\[
\mu^{*t}(g)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_\chi\chi(1)\overline{\chi(g)}\,\Bigl(\frac{\hat\mu(\chi)}{\chi(1)}\Bigr)^t,\qquad\hat\mu(\chi)=\sum_{h\in G}\mu(h)\chi(h),
\]
the sum being over the irreducible characters of $G$. (Show first that, for a class function $f$ and an irreducible representation $\rho$ of
dimension $d$, the matrix $\sum_hf(h)\rho(h)$ is the scalar $\frac1d\sum_hf(h)\chi_\rho(h)$.)
\item Using the character table of $A_5$ (Exercise~11.7), show that the icosahedron is back in its initial position after $t$
turns with probability
\[
\frac1{60}\Bigl(1+16\cdot4^{-t}+25\cdot\Bigl(-\frac15\Bigr)^t\Bigr).
\]
\item Find the probability that after $t$ turns the icosahedron has turned by a fifth of a turn (in either direction) about some
axis through opposite vertices, and show that the law of the position converges to the uniform law at the rate $4^{-t}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}
exercise_changes.new_statement:
\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{pb:dodecaturns}
\emph{Random turns of an icosahedron.} The rotation group of the regular icosahedron is isomorphic to $A_5$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteso3}), and the
$20$ rotations by a third of a turn about the axes through the centres of opposite faces form the conjugacy class of the
$3$-cycles. An icosahedron is turned, again and again, by a uniformly chosen one of these $20$ rotations.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $\mu$ be a probability on a finite group $G$ that is constant on conjugacy classes, and $\mu^{*t}$ the law of the walk at integer time
$t\ge0$, started at $e$. Show that, for every $g\in G$,
\[
\mu^{*t}(g)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_\chi\chi(1)\overline{\chi(g)}\,\Bigl(\frac{\hat\mu(\chi)}{\chi(1)}\Bigr)^t,\qquad\hat\mu(\chi)=\sum_{h\in G}\mu(h)\chi(h),
\]
the sum being over the irreducible characters of $G$. At $t=0$ interpret every scalar's zeroth power as $1$, including $0^0$, because it comes from the zeroth matrix power. (Show first that, for a class function $f$ and an irreducible representation $\rho$ of
dimension $d$, the matrix $\sum_hf(h)\rho(h)$ is the scalar $\frac1d\sum_hf(h)\chi_\rho(h)$.)
\item Using the character table of $A_5$ (Exercise~\ref{ex:a5}), find the return probability for every $t\ge0$. Show that for $t\ge1$ it simplifies to
\[
\frac1{60}\Bigl(1+16\cdot4^{-t}+25\cdot\Bigl(-\frac15\Bigr)^t\Bigr).
\]
\item Find the probability that after $t\ge0$ turns the icosahedron has turned by a fifth of a turn (in either direction) about some
axis through opposite vertices, and show that the law of the position converges to the uniform law at the rate $4^{-t}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}

main_changes.old_statement: The preimages of these groups in $S^3$ are the \emph{binary} polyhedral groups, of orders $24$, $48$ and $120$ (Exercises~\ref{ex:2T} and~\ref{ex:2I}). The binary icosahedral group $2I$, of order $120$, is especially rich: the quotient $S^3/2I$ is the Poincaré homology sphere, a $3$-manifold with the same homology as $S^3$ but a different fundamental group, and the $120$ elements of $2I$ are the vertices of the regular $4$-dimensional polytope called the $600$-cell. These connections, found one by one over a century, are still being explored.
main_changes.new_statement:
The preimages of the tetrahedral, cube and icosahedral groups in $S^3$
are the \emph{binary polyhedral groups}, of orders $24$, $48$ and $120$:
each rotation has two lifts. Exercises~\ref{ex:2T} and~\ref{ex:2I} examine
the first and last of these groups. The signs retain real algebraic information.
For instance a spatial half-turn has a pure unit lift $u$, so $u^2=-1$;
its lift has order four even though the rotation has order two.
main_changes.reason: Keep binary-group orders/kernel/order-four lifts. Remove unproved homology-sphere and600-cell excursion from the teaching route.

main_changes.new_statement:
\begin{beauty}
Take a fifth-turn rotation of the icosahedron. Its spatial trace is
$1+2\cos(2\pi/5)=\varphi$, the golden ratio in the character table.
One unit-quaternion lift has real part $\cos(\pi/5)=\varphi/2$, so its
complex $2\times2$ matrix also has trace $\varphi$.
The other lift has trace $-\varphi$, while giving exactly the same spatial
rotation. The formula $4(\varphi/2)^2-1=\varphi$ checks both descriptions.

The finite group behind these motions is $A_5$. Chapter~4 proves its simplicity, and Section~\ref{tool:smallest-simple} proves its minimal order.
The final workshop returns to the same group with random turns: the numbers
in its character table will measure how quickly the initial orientation
is forgotten. The appendices then use linear algebra and symmetry to count
and to control the signs of eigenvalues.
\end{beauty}

main_changes.new_statement:
\begin{remark}[a first look at categories]
A homomorphism $f:G\to H$ sends $[x,y]$ to $[f(x),f(y)]$, hence sends
$G'$ into $H'$ and induces $G/G'\to H/H'$. The identity induces the
identity, and a composite induces the composite. This is an example of a
\emph{functor}. A \emph{category} specifies objects, maps between them,
identity maps and associative composition; groups with homomorphisms are
one example. A functor assigns new objects and maps while preserving those
two composition rules. Thus abelianization $G\mapsto G/G'$ is a functor.
Likewise a homomorphism between commutative rings $R,S$ acts on polynomial coefficients, giving $R[X]\to S[X]$, and coefficientwise calculation checks the same rules.
For finite abelian groups the dual reverses maps: $f:A\to B$ induces
$\widehat B\to\widehat A$, $\chi\mapsto\chi\circ f$.
For $h:B\to C$, associativity gives $(h\circ f)^*=f^*\circ h^*$; this reversed order is why it is called a \emph{contravariant functor}. These examples introduce the language;
no category-theoretic theorem is used in our proofs.
\end{remark}
main_changes.reason: Define category/functor and prove actual map-on-maps examples and reversed dual composition. Do not classify an unexplained element-level homomorphism as an object-level functor.
main_changes.loss: Unneeded unverified historical date and future-volume pointer; actual concepts/examples strengthened.

main_changes.old_statement: Composing rotations is multiplying quaternions (Exercise~\ref{ex:compose}): four numbers instead of nine, no drift away from orthogonality that cannot be cured by dividing by the norm, and smooth interpolation between orientations. This is why flight software, robots and video games store orientations as unit quaternions.
main_changes.new_statement:
Composing rotations is multiplying quaternions (Exercise~\ref{ex:compose}):
four coordinates encode the orientation. A nonzero numerical approximation
$r$ can be made unit again by replacing it with $r/|r|$, where
$|r|=\sqrt{N(r)}$.
There is also a direct smooth interpolation. For unit representatives
$q_0,q_1$, replace $q_1$ by $-q_1$ if necessary so that their ordinary
four-coordinate dot product is nonnegative. Put
\[
r(t)=(1-t)q_0+tq_1,\qquad q(t)=r(t)/|r(t)|,\quad0\le t\le1.
\]
Then $|r(t)|^2\ge(1-t)^2+t^2\ge1/2$, so division never fails and the
formulas give a smooth path of unit quaternions between the two orientations.
Shoemake's source below develops quaternion interpolation for animation.
main_changes.reason: N is squared length, so normalize nonzero r bysqrt(N(r)). Earn smooth interpolation by sign choice and norm-squared>=1/2.

main_changes.old_statement: Taking norms in $(a+bi+cj+dk)(a'+b'i+c'j+d'k)$ gives Euler's four-square identity (Exercise~\ref{ex:euler4}), used in Volume~2 to reduce the four-square theorem to primes. Frobenius proved in 1878 that $\R$, $\C$ and $\mathbb H$ are the only finite-dimensional associative division algebras over $\R$; dropping associativity adds Cayley's octonions, of dimension $8$, and nothing else.
main_changes.new_statement: Taking norms in $(a+bi+cj+dk)(a'+b'i+c'j+d'k)$ gives Euler's four-square identity (Exercise~\ref{ex:euler4}), used in Volume~2 to reduce the four-square theorem to primes. A classification result beyond our proofs is Frobenius's theorem: $\R$, $\C$ and $\mathbb H$ are the only finite-dimensional associative division algebras over $\R$. Dropping associativity alone does not give a comparable list. For finite-dimensional real algebras with an identity and a squared Euclidean length satisfying $N(xy)=N(x)N(y)$, Hurwitz's theorem gives $\R$, $\C$, $\mathbb H$ and the eight-dimensional octonions. Neither classification is a premise below.
